questions.q: What does `delegatecall` let a proxy contract do?
options: Deploy a brand-new contract automatically
Run another contract's (the implementation's) code inside the proxy's own storage context
Permanently merge two contracts into one address
Skip paying gas for external calls
questions.explain: delegatecall executes the implementation's logic but reads/writes the proxy's own storage, which is what makes 'upgrading' possible without moving data.

questions.q: What actually changes when a proxy-based contract is "upgraded"?
options: The proxy's address changes to a new one
All existing storage is wiped and reset
The proxy is pointed at a new implementation address — its own address and storage stay the same
A brand-new proxy is deployed for every upgrade
questions.explain: Upgrading means updating which implementation address the proxy delegatecalls into — the proxy's address (what users interact with) and its storage never change.

questions.q: How do Transparent, UUPS, and Beacon proxy patterns primarily differ, according to this lesson?
options: They use entirely different low-level call mechanisms
In who's allowed to trigger an upgrade and where that authorization check lives
Only Beacon proxies support Solidity
UUPS doesn't use delegatecall at all
questions.explain: All three rely on delegatecall underneath; they differ in where the upgrade-authorization check lives — the proxy itself (Transparent), the implementation (UUPS), or a shared beacon (Beacon).

questions.q: Why do UUPS upgradeable contracts use an `initialize()` function with an `initializer` modifier instead of a constructor?
options: Solidity doesn't support constructors at all
A constructor's state changes apply to the implementation's own storage at deploy time, never to the proxy's storage that's actually used
initialize() is required by the EVM for all contracts
Constructors cost more gas than initialize functions
questions.explain: Since the proxy delegatecalls into the implementation, a constructor run during the implementation's own deployment never touches the proxy's storage — initialize() run through the proxy does.

questions.q: What happens if a UUPS contract's `_authorizeUpgrade` function is left unprotected (no access control)?
options: Nothing — it's purely a style convention
The contract automatically becomes immutable
Anyone can call it to point the proxy at arbitrary, potentially malicious implementation logic
The proxy stops working entirely
questions.explain: _authorizeUpgrade is the actual gate controlling who can swap the implementation — unprotected, it lets any caller redirect the proxy to malicious logic.
